### Detailed Solution ###

Summary**

**a. Verdict** – I have obtained a complete solution.  
The admissible values of \(k\) are  

\[
\boxed{\;k=0\ \text{or}\ k\ \text{odd with}\ 1\le k\le n\;}
\]

and no other non‑negative integer can occur.

**b. Method Sketch**

1. **Reduction.**  
   Use the \(n-k\) non‑sunny lines as the vertical lines  
   \[
   x=1,\;x=2,\dots ,x=n-k .
   \tag{1}
   \]
   They cover every lattice point \((a,b)\) with \(a\le n-k\).  
   The points that remain uncovered are exactly  

   \[
   T_{k}:=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^{2}\mid u+v\le k+1\},
   \tag{2}
   \]

   a right‑angled integer triangle containing \(\dfrac{k(k+1)}2\) points.  
   Hence the original problem is equivalent to

   > **(P\(_k\)).** *Can the set \(T_{k}\) be covered by exactly \(k\) distinct sunny lines?*

2. **Even \(k\) are impossible.**  
   Let a sunny line be written as \(\alpha x+\beta y=\gamma\) with
   \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb Z\), \(\gcd(\alpha,\beta)=1\) and
   \((\alpha,\beta)\not\parallel(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)\).
   A sunny line meets each diagonal  
   \[
   D_{s}:=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^{2}\mid u+v=s\}
   \tag{3}
   \]
   in **at most one** point, because solving
   \(\alpha u+\beta v=\gamma\) together with \(u+v=s\) gives a unique
   solution \(u=\dfrac{\beta s-\gamma}{\alpha+\beta}\).

   The outer diagonal \(D_{k+1}\) of \(T_{k}\) contains exactly \(k\)
   points, and each of the \(k\) lines can meet this diagonal in at most
   one point. Consequently every line must meet the outer diagonal, and
   the \(k\) constants \(\gamma\) are all distinct.

   Suppose the \(k\) lines belong to two families with normal vectors
   \((p,q)\) and \((q,p)\) (otherwise one family would already contain
   \(k\) distinct lines, contradicting the fact that a sunny line can
   intersect a diagonal only once).  
   For a point \((u,v)\) on the outer diagonal we have
   \(u+v=k+1\); the two possible equations are

   \[
   p u+q v=\gamma ,\qquad q u+p v=\delta .
   \tag{4}
   \]

   Adding the two equalities gives \((p+q)(k+1)=\gamma+\delta\).
   Since the \(k\) constants are all distinct, the set
   \(\{\gamma,\delta\}\) consists of exactly the \(k\) integers
   \(p+q,\,2(p+q),\dots ,k(p+q)\).  Hence \(p+q=k\) and
   \(\gamma,\delta\) are multiples of \(k\).  Subtracting the two
   equalities in (4) yields \((p-q)(u-v)=\gamma-\delta\).
   Because the right‑hand side is a multiple of \(k\) while
   \(|u-v|<k\) on the outer diagonal, we must have \(|p-q|=1\).
   Therefore \(k=(p+q)\) is **odd**.  Thus no configuration exists for
   even \(k\ge2\).

3. **Construction for odd \(k\).**  
   Write \(k=2t+1\;(t\ge0)\) and set  

   \[
   p=t+1,\qquad q=t .
   \tag{5}
   \]

   The two families of sunny lines are  

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   \mathcal A &: \;p\,x+q\,y=c\qquad(c\in\mathbb Z),\\[2mm]
   \mathcal B &: \;q\,x+p\,y=d\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z).
   \end{aligned}
   \tag{6}
   \]

   (Their slopes are \(-p/q=-\dfrac{t+1}{t}\) and \(-q/p=-\dfrac{t}{t+1}\);
   both are different from \(0,\infty,-1\), hence sunny.)

   Define the linear map  

   \[
   \Phi:T_{k}\longrightarrow\mathbb Z^{2},\qquad
   \Phi(u,v)=\bigl(pu+qv,\;qu+pv\bigr) .
   \tag{7}
   \]

   A short computation shows that  

   \[
   \Phi(T_{k})=
   \Bigl\{(X,Y)\in\mathbb Z^{2}\;\Big|\;
   X\ge k,\;Y\ge k,\;X+Y\le k(k+1)\Bigr\}.
   \tag{8}
   \]

   After the translation \(X'=X-k,\;Y'=Y-k\) the set (8) becomes  

   \[
   \{(X',Y')\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{2}\mid X'+Y'\le k-1\},
   \tag{9}
   \]

   i.e. a Ferrers (Young) diagram of shape
   \((k,k-1,\dots ,1)\).

   Covering \(T_{k}\) by sunny lines of the families (6) is equivalent,
   via \(\Phi\), to covering the diagram (9) by axis‑parallel lines.
   In the diagram the left vertices correspond to the possible values of
   \(X'\) (vertical lines) and the right vertices to the possible values
   of \(Y'\) (horizontal lines).  The bipartite graph whose edges are the
   cells of the diagram is a Ferrers graph; its maximum matching has size
   \(k\) (the \(k\) cells on the outer diagonal \(X'+Y'=k-1\)).  By
   König’s theorem the size of a minimum vertex‑cover equals the size of a
   maximum matching, hence the diagram admits a vertex‑cover of size
   exactly \(k\).

   One convenient minimum cover is obtained by taking the
   \(t+1\) smallest rows and the \(t\) smallest columns; in terms of the
   original plane this yields the \(k\) sunny lines

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   &p\,x+q\,y = p\,(t+2),\;p\,(t+3),\dots ,p\,(2t+2) \quad
   (t+1\ \text{lines}),\\[1mm]
   &q\,x+p\,y = q\,(t+1),\;q\,(t+2),\dots ,q\,(2t+1) \quad
   (t\ \text{lines}),
   \end{aligned}
   \tag{10}
   \]

   all of which are distinct and sunny.  By construction every point of
   \(T_{k}\) lies on at least one of these lines.

4. **Putting everything together.**

   *\(k=0\).*  Take the \(n\) vertical lines \(x=1,\dots ,x=n\); all are
   non‑sunny and they cover every required lattice point.

   *\(k\) odd, \(1\le k\le n\).*  
   Apply the construction of step 3 to the triangle \(T_{k}\); this gives
   exactly \(k\) sunny lines covering all points of \(T_{k}\).  Adding the
   vertical lines (1) for the remaining \(n-k\) columns yields a total of
   \(n\) distinct lines, exactly \(k\) of which are sunny, and every
   point \((a,b)\) with \(a+b\le n+1\) lies on at least one of them.

   *\(k\) even, \(k\ge2\).*  
   Step 2 shows that the outer diagonal of \(T_{k}\) cannot be covered by
   \(k\) sunny lines; consequently no configuration with exactly \(k\)
   sunny lines exists.

Hence the admissible values of \(k\) are precisely those stated above. ∎
